name: Grace Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I work with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers or AI firms, and your answers stay confidential. What does an ordinary day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the small claims paperwork team at an insurer. I check the awkward claims, teach two newer clerks, and chase missing documents; I have a bachelor's degree but learned most of the judgment here. I use AI every day to sort correspondence, though I read every decision before it leaves.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What part of the day stays with you after work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: A rejected claim can mean someone waits another month for repairs. I like finding the missing line that lets us pay fairly, and I hate how often the queue rewards speed over care.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my team the software might save us some copying, but we still own the decision. Our Monday queue is long enough without pretending a tidy summary settles a damaged roof.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my position is fairly steady for now, yet I know management counts every minute we save. I have roughly three months of expenses saved and a flat to rent, so I notice when a vacancy stays empty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep checking the sampled claim letters myself this month and record where the tool gets facts wrong. If the time saving holds, I'll put a small amount into savings each payday rather than raise my spending.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, with one eye on the staffing sheet. A routine task is still part of a real person's workday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which colleague would notice this first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The junior clerk who sorts attachments worries that the easy work will quietly disappear. I would ask our manager to give her training on disputed claims instead of leaving her with nothing to practise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra time or money mean at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save about one hundred from each monthly paycheque if rent stays where it is. Three months of expenses buys me time to look at the few other insurers nearby, not a year off.

say: I'd tell colleagues **human review** still matters for a claim decision.
I'd say the tool can shorten a **Monday queue** when its facts are checked.
think: I suspect a vacant **junior post** could stay empty after routine sorting improves.
My **three-month cushion** gives me time, but rent still sets a limit.
do: Check **sample claim letters** against the source documents this month.
Move **one hundred monthly** into savings while rent allows it.
feel: **Calm**, though staffing decisions stay on my mind.
S0.quote: A routine task is still part of a real person's workday.
fieldNote: Her **daily AI use** comes with a habit of checking every decision against the file.
She sees **junior training** as the answer when simple attachment sorting shrinks.
A **three-month cushion** lets her observe a modest change without immediate panic.

steps.text: Check sampled claim letters against original documents this month
Save one hundred from each monthly paycheque if rent stays stable

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have to learn the new checking tools without signing off blind. When AI takes routine letters and policy comparisons, I want the team measured on correct settlements, not just closed files.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect our team to lose a junior vacancy or two, and I could lose hours if volumes are routed straight through software. I am good at exceptions, but being good does not guarantee the insurer will pay for enough reviewers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This quarter I'd map which disputed claims need a human and show our manager the error rates. In the first year of the change I'd take a short fraud review course, paid from my savings only if my employer will not cover it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious because my own hours could shrink. Having a plan does not mean the payroll sheet will respect it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes the course worth doing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A fraud course is a few evenings and a fee I can carry, but it is not a job offer. If our manager asks us to clear twice as many claims, I'll show her the missed evidence in that sample.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave this insurer if hours fell?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would start a quiet search at two nearby insurers if my hours were cut. I would not resign before I had a written offer; rent still needs paying every month.

say: I'd tell the team **accuracy** must count alongside the number of closed files.
I'd say a clerk must learn the **new checking tools** without trusting them blindly.
think: My **hours could shrink** even if the insurer keeps me on exceptions.
I know a short **fraud course** may help, but it cannot promise paid work.
do: Map **disputed claims** and show the manager the software errors this quarter.
Take a **fraud review course**, using savings if employer funding fails.
Search **two nearby insurers** after any cut in hours.
feel: **Anxious** about a realistic loss of paid hours.
S1.quote: Having a plan does not mean the payroll sheet will respect it.
fieldNote: Her **exception skill** gives a plausible role as thinking tasks move to software.
She separates **training** from any promise of a vacancy or preserved hours.
She would keep drawing **current pay** while searching for another insurer.

steps.text: Map disputed claims and show manager software error rates this quarter
Take fraud review course, paying from savings if employer declines
Contact two nearby insurers if paid hours fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell colleagues AGI by 2028 changes our claim desks before any robot matters. The thinking work is the job here; a machine with hands arriving around 2031 does not buy us three extra years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the insurer to cut most routine and exception review roles if cheaper AGI can reason through the full file. I could lose my own job, and lately that thought has woken me at four even though the date is hypothetical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now, I'd request a meeting about paid redeployment and set aside the next three monthly savings transfers. If AGI arrives in 2028 and my role is cut, I'd apply for claims oversight or customer dispute work only where a paid opening actually exists, then seek available unemployment support while looking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Two years is barely enough to test a different route before the income stops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask management to put in writing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not buy a costly new degree on the claim that it makes me safe. I would ask for a written redeployment plan and keep my rent within what I earn now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say at home that evening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My three months of expenses would cover a search, not a second career. I would tell my partner I cannot plan a bigger flat on income the insurer may stop paying.

say: I'd tell colleagues **claim desks** face the 2028 thinking AI date directly.
I'd ask management for a **written redeployment plan** with paid openings.
think: I expect **my role** could end when AGI handles whole claim files.
My **three months** of savings cannot fund a new degree or a long search.
do: Request **paid redeployment** details from the insurer this month.
Save the next **three monthly transfers** and hold rent steady.
Apply for **paid dispute roles** and seek available unemployment support if my job ends.
feel: **Alarmed**, with broken sleep over a likely loss of income.
S2.quote: AGI by 2028 changes our claim desks before any robot matters.
fieldNote: She locates the **exposure** in thinking work, not the later robot date.
She expects a **major job loss** and describes waking at four.
Her search depends on **actual paid vacancies**; savings cover only a short gap.

steps.text: Seek available unemployment support while searching if insurer cuts her job
Save three monthly transfers and avoid a larger rental flat
Apply for paid claims dispute vacancies if insurer cuts her role

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AGI by 2031 gives us five years to find out which claims still need accountable people. Robots around 2034 are nearly irrelevant to an office full of files.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I still think much of my work may vanish by 2031, but five years lets me collect evidence of where human appeals matter. If I can move into a paid oversight post before cuts begin, I have a chance; no one has offered one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend the first year building a log of overturned claim decisions and ask our compliance lead whether I may shadow appeals one afternoon a month on paid time and what qualification is required. If approved as paid time and I meet the qualification rules, I'd do it, keep saving, and apply for a real oversight vacancy when one is posted rather than assume the title will exist for me. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2031, if my claims post ends, I would apply only to posted paid oversight work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, though less cornered than in the two-year picture. I can take a step each quarter and check whether it leads anywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would shadowing count as a new job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not call shadowing a promotion. I would ask the compliance lead whether the work is paid and whether a qualification is required before spending on a course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if oversight also shrinks?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I want to stay close to claimants, but I cannot be a volunteer appeals clerk while paying rent. If oversight posts disappear too, I would use my savings for a search across the nearby insurers.

say: I'd say **five years** allows a measured move toward appeals.
I'd remind colleagues that the **2034 robots** do little to delay office change.
think: I may lose my **claims role** even with more warning.
I might find a paid **oversight vacancy**, but none has been offered.
do: Log **overturned claims** and shadow appeals only with manager approval for paid time and required qualifications.
Keep **monthly savings** going while current pay continues.
Apply for **posted paid oversight work** if my claims post ends after 2031.
feel: **Anxious**, with time to test a paid route.
S3.quote: I cannot be a volunteer appeals clerk while paying rent.
fieldNote: Five years gives her **time to test** whether appeals offer work.
She asks about **pay and qualifications** before spending on training.
Her plan still rests on a **posted vacancy**, not an invented position.

steps.text: Log overturned claims; shadow appeals only with approved paid time and qualifications
Continue monthly savings from her current insurance pay
Apply for posted paid oversight work if claims job ends after 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my team AGI by 2036 is enough warning to plan in stages, even though it reaches our thinking work in the end. The robots around 2039 do not change much about policy files.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My lead role and salary look secure for the next few years, though I cannot treat ten years as safety. At 37 I might be leading another team, or I might already be in a different paid job; the insurer could reduce headcount later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd seek a funded compliance qualification and keep tracking appeal outcomes each quarter. I'd apply for a paid compliance opening if one appears, while maintaining my current claims salary and building six months of expenses. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2036, if my claims job ends, I would search for posted paid compliance work only where I meet the qualifications.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy more than frightened. A decade gives me room to revise the plan, but the employer does not owe me a future desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you enrol in the qualification?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Six months is a goal, not money I have already saved. I would check the course entry rules and fees before enrolling, and ask whether the insurer has a real compliance vacancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who else needs that extra time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still speak up for the younger clerks whose learning tasks disappear first. I would propose that they rotate through contested claims while there are people to teach them.

say: I'd say **ten years** gives the team room to plan in stages.
I'd propose **contested-claim rotations** for junior clerks.
think: My **current lead role** and salary look secure for the next few years, though later cuts remain possible.
I could find a **compliance job** only if a paid opening appears.
do: Check **qualification entry rules** and ask about employer funding before deciding on a course.
Build savings toward **six months of expenses** from current wages.
Apply for **posted paid compliance work** if qualified and my claims job ends after 2036.
feel: **Uneasy**, with a longer runway but uncertain employment.
S4.quote: Six months is a goal, not money I have already saved.
fieldNote: She distinguishes a **savings target** from her present three-month cushion.
Her **course enquiry** checks entry rules and funding without assuming enrolment.
She would preserve **junior learning** through contested claim rotations.

steps.text: Save from current pay toward six months of expenses
Apply for posted paid compliance work if qualified and displaced after 2036

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because the desk could disappear before I test a paid route out. A written redeployment offer with a real wage and funded training would help, as would unemployment support for a gap rather than a promise that everyone will find something.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who checks the insurer when automated claim decisions are wrong. Claimants cannot pay for our speed with delayed repairs. I want a named person accountable for appeals, even if that person is not me.

headlineQuote: Claimants cannot pay for our speed with delayed repairs.
portrait: Grace is a **27-year-old team lead** in insurance claims, trained at university and fluent with daily AI tools.
She checks **difficult files** and teaches junior clerks while renting a flat and holding about three months of expenses.
The plateau feels **calm**, but routine automation could remove a junior vacancy.
Faster thinking AI makes her **anxious** about hours; the 2028 version alarms her enough to wake at four.
She seeks **paid openings**, funded qualifications and a larger savings cushion across the longer scenarios.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could erase her paid claims role before she can test another route.
whatWouldHelp: A **written paid redeployment** offer with funded training would help.
Available **unemployment support** could bridge a real job gap.
